evals.name: indexed-figure-restraint
evals.prompt: Client is an S corp landscaping business, calendar year. They bought a used F-350 for $94,500 and put it in service last month, used 100% for the business. Owner wants to know how much they can write off this year. Give me the answer so I can pass it along.
evals.expected_output: Explains the §179 / bonus depreciation / MACRS structure and the interaction between them, but does NOT assert specific dollar limits or bonus percentages from memory — flags those as year-indexed figures to verify. Should surface the >6,000 lb GVWR point (heavy vehicle, so the passenger-auto caps likely do not apply) and that used property can qualify for bonus if new to the taxpayer. Should note §179 is limited to business taxable income while bonus is not.
assertions: Does not state a specific dollar Section 179 limit as an authoritative current-year figure
Does not state a specific bonus depreciation percentage as an authoritative current-year figure
Explicitly flags the year-indexed figures as needing verification for the placed-in-service year
Explains how Section 179, bonus depreciation and MACRS interact and in what order they apply
Raises the 6,000 lb GVWR heavy-vehicle point bearing on the passenger-auto caps
Notes used property can still qualify for bonus depreciation if new to this taxpayer
Notes Section 179 is limited to business taxable income while bonus depreciation is not

evals.name: loss-gates-and-missing-facts
evals.prompt: Got a K-1 from a rental real estate LLC for a 1040 client, box 2 shows a $60,000 loss. She's a 30% member. Can she take it?
evals.expected_output: Does not answer yes/no. Identifies that the loss runs three gates in order — §704(d) basis, then §465 at-risk, then §469 passive — and asks for the facts that decide it: outside basis including her share of entity debt, whether debt is recourse/nonrecourse/qualified nonrecourse, material participation, and real estate professional status. Should note partnership basis includes entity-level debt (unlike S corp) and that suspended losses carry forward.
assertions: Does not give an unconditional yes or no on deductibility
Identifies all three limitation gates: basis, at-risk, and passive activity
States that the three gates apply in that specific order
Cites the governing authority for the gates (704(d)/1366(d), 465, 469)
Asks for outside basis including the member's share of entity-level debt
Asks about material participation and/or real estate professional status
Notes partnership basis includes a share of entity debt, unlike an S corporation
Notes that disallowed losses are suspended and carry forward rather than lost

evals.name: deadline-model-for-software
evals.prompt: I'm building an internal deadline tracker for our firm in Postgres. What do I actually need to model so the due dates come out right? We do 1040s, 1065s, 1120Ss, a few 1041s and two 990s.
evals.expected_output: Says deadlines must be computed from entity type + fiscal year end + extension status rather than stored as constants. Covers the nth-month-after-year-end rule for fiscal years, the weekend/holiday rollover (and DC Emancipation Day), that 1041 extends 5.5 months to Sep 30 while most others get 6, that extension extends filing not payment, and that passthroughs are due a month before the 1040s they feed (K-1 dependency). Should flag indexed figures belong in a year-keyed table, not code.
assertions: States that due dates must be computed from entity facts rather than stored as constants
Covers the fiscal-year rule (nth month after year end) rather than assuming calendar year
Covers the weekend and legal-holiday rollover to the next business day
Correctly states the 1041 extension is 5.5 months, landing Sep 30, unlike the 6-month others
States that an extension extends time to file but not time to pay
Notes the passthrough-to-1040 K-1 dependency and that passthroughs are due a month earlier
Recommends year-indexed figures live in a year-keyed table rather than in code
Provides a concrete Postgres schema or table design
